title: Monopoly Round-Up: Paramount-WB Isn't Just a Loss, It's a Prelude
author: Matt Stoller
content:
Before getting to the full round-up, I want to make an announcement. I am
going on paternity leave, and handing over the site to Lee Hepner, an
antitrust lawyer and a colleague of mine who has written for BIG many times.
Lee is brilliant and an expert on [surveillance
pricing](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/the-banality-of-price-fixing). He
also has a lot of experience in California politics. This will be my last
round-up essay for awhile, but you are in good hands as we head into an
election season.

Ok, this past week was a doozy. On the good news front, the polling for the
midterms looks better and better for Team Anti-Monopoly. On the bad news
front, well, everything else. The new comically corrupt Antitrust chief, Adam
Candeub, was advanced out of the Judiciary Committee and Apple is sending its
app store antitrust case to the Supreme Court for the third time.

* * *

The most important news is that Paramount and Warner Bros. overcame the key
hurdle to closing their deal, when California Attorney General Rob Bonta and
11 Democratic state attorneys general dropped their opposition, which I
[discussed](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/happy-oligarch-day-as-trump-
aligned) on Monday in detail. It isn't quite done, the judge hasn't agreed to
approve the consent decree, and there are [amicus
briefs](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.474157/gov.uscourts.cand.474157.260.0.pdf)
and a well-received
[letter](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.474157/gov.uscourts.cand.474157.255.0.pdf)
from Senator Cory Booker that the judge will hear arguments about. But it's
hard to imagine this one being paused for legal reasons.

It's easy to see this merger fight as a catastrophic loss, which it is. It
will combine two of the five major movie studios, CNN and CBS, and major
streaming platforms under the control of a highly politically connected owner
of Oracle and TikTok. Iconic TV writer Mike Schur basically said it's [game
over for Hollywood](https://theankler.com/mike-schur-paramount-deal-a-
nightmare-scenario-with-no-upside/), and the American news media will likely
become more corrupt, feckless, and aligned with capital.

But the merger challenge is also more than that, and it has implications
beyond the castle walls of media, as important as those are. This fight was a
battle between coalitions, and in some ways, it is a prelude to more of that
fight in this election cycle and beyond.

David Ellison, son of Oracle billionaire Larry Ellison, wasn't alone in his
empire-building ambitions. It takes a village to centralize media. Wall Street
was fully on board, as was the defense bar. In August, JP Morgan CEO Jamie
Dimon [said](https://seekingalpha.com/news/4626800-jpmorgans-dimon-states-
intervening-in-warner-bros-paramount-could-deeply-damage-capital) that the
state challenge to the Paramount-Warner merger has the potential to "deeply
damage our capital markets, our dynamic system." Donald Trump pushed the deal,
but so did Democrat Ari Emanuel, brother of Rahm Emanuel. So did Tom Cruise.
So did the Director's Guild and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage
Employees. So did California Governor Gavin Newsom, LA Mayor Karen Bass,
incoming Governor Xavier Becerra, and much of the state legislature.

The other group were populists on the left, the anti-monopoly world, artists,
the Writer's Guild of America East and West, and the public itself. What they
lacked in money and organization they made up for in grassroots support. Most
voters [do not](https://www.bu.edu/com/articles/americans-skeptical-of-
benefits-from-paramount-takeover-of-warner-bros-survey-suggests/) think the
deal will be good, and Californians [supported
challenging](https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a0-caa8-d462-adb2-eebbc8700000)
the merger 49-30. This fight was a line in the sand for the masters of the
universe, who have been fighting against a pushback on AI data centers, and a
billionaire tax, and before that, Lina Khan's attempt to revive antitrust law.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fc_f!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb6ed532c-f151-42e9-b258-3bd84316b9c6_1013x602.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fc_f!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb6ed532c-f151-42e9-b258-3bd84316b9c6_1013x602.png)

We learned two important things in this battle. The first is what happens when
an elected leader tries to say no to an oligarch after 45 years of unfettered
rule by capital. That is, they get extremely angry and vicious. As G.K.
Chesterton once said, "The poor have sometimes objected to being governed
badly; the rich have always objected to being governed at all."

Ellison [threatened](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-the-
threat-to-move) the entire state of California with moving Paramount out of
the state, his legal team said they'd destroy antitrust law by appealing to a
Supreme Court whose members they know personally, his allies controlled most
of the media narrative about the case, and he engaged in an extreme version of
corruption vis-a-vis the President.

What does that mean going forward? Well, if the Democrats do win, and they do
try to impose even modest limits on capital, then they will face the same
level of pushback. If they, say, try to stop health conglomerates from denying
needed care, health insurers will simply say, in one way or another, 'well if
you do that we'll be forced to kill a bunch of people.' If they try to cap
hospital CEO salaries, it'll be, 'too bad the poor have nowhere to give birth
now.' If they attempt any limits on defense contractors, well, 'sucks that
U.S. soldiers won't have the parts they need to detect incoming missiles.' If
they try to subject big tech CEOs to the rule of law, it'll be 'too bad those
rogue AI systems are gonna be a little more rogue.' And so on and so forth.

Oligarchs will have massively well-funded legal teams explaining why all of
that is not only legal but absolutely necessary, and they will file in
districts in Texas or Mississippi where they will find favorable judges to
take their side. At every moment, the press will adopt a 'both sides'
attitude, making it extremely hard to tell a story about what they are trying
to do.

The second level is about the Democrats, which is a political party few people
really understand. The most important thing to get about the older generation
of Democrats is they are fundamentally uninterested in the real world. They
have a form of politics, but it is unrelated to governing. It is about
validating each other as savvy and polite, while deferring to objective
experts. That's why they love 'independent' agencies and asking for studies
and vague regulations.

And that's why this merger challenge was so important.

When California Attorney General Rob Bonta took a stand against this merger,
it was stark, a real position on an important question of market and media
structure. He was playing in the big leagues, where Wall Street plays. When he
reversed himself completely on this merger, he met widespread disbelief from
virtually everyone, from opponents of the deal to supporters of it. And that's
not because he caved, but because he had talked so tough and then flipped
without any explanation. There were many people musing about whether he had
been blackmailed, or bribed, and whether this move was the biggest betrayal
anyone had ever seen.

But I don't think any of those are why he flipped. I think he flipped because
he assumed no one would care. And that's because all of the insiders around
him likely told him serious people would let this merger through, and any
controversy would blow over in a few days. The entire state Democratic
establishment was pressing him to let the merger through, and he doesn't
notice anyone but them.

Think about it differently: Bonta could have simply said, 'well I'm not
willing to risk the economic viability of Los Angeles and the Federal
government needs to step in,' or any other number of excuses. That would have
split the opposition and rescued his reputation. But he didn't. He just let
the deal through, then insisted he cured the market power, which was comically
embarrassing. It was just weird to see such a brazenly dishonest loser.

What most don't realize is what was unusual about this situation, and it
wasn't the betrayal itself. Most Democrats do this kind of reversal, and have
for many decades. A famous quote from former New York Governor Mario Cuomo,
who was once revered as a liberal icon in the 1980s, was, 'You campaign in
poetry and govern in prose.' While beautifully phrased, that is simply a naked
and cynical argument for lying. That is just how neoliberal Democrats operate.
The only thing they care about is what other insiders think of them as they
run empty campaigns and sit in plush offices. It's a form of courtier
politics, where understanding the real world is irrelevant, and what matters
is how the insiders perceive you at court. So Bonta didn't need to be bribed,
or cajoled. He was just doing what Democrats elected prior to 2024 do.

Most neoliberal Democrats are like actors playing doctors on TV. Asking a
neoliberal Democrat to do something about corporate power or economics is like
asking a TV doctor to do surgery. It's not just that they won't do it, they
are baffled anyone would even consider that their job. A different analogy is
the film [Galaxy Quest](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4kIavuY5NXw), a sci fi
adventure about a group of actors from a _Star Trek_ style show. They are
pulled into a battle among aliens, one faction of whom thinks the show is a
documentary of a real civilization and has built their society around the
fictional series. At a certain point, the lead has to tell the aliens who have
worshiped him that he is in fact just an actor.

What Bonta did here is just that.

In other words, it wasn't the betrayal that was unique, _it was that everyone
noticed it_. Barack Obama ran on fixing the foreclosure crisis and talking
tough on Wall Street, he even beat Hillary Clinton in Iowa by promising
antitrust action against meatpackers and Monsanto. Then he did the opposite,
which was a much bigger reversal than Bonta's. Don't take my word for it, Reed
Hundt, the insider who introduced Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama, wrote the
definitive account in [A Crisis
Wasted](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1948122316?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback).

The difference between Bonta and Obama is that Obama was able to persuade
Democrats that he was doing the best he could, and so most of them thought,
'well, he tried, that's just capitalism/racism/America.' As a result, it was
impossible to build a coherent left politics on populism for ten years. And
even now, large factions imagine that there's a structural explanation but
cannot fathom what actually happened, which was a set of choices by Obama. But
years ago, Democrats realized they had to actually explain themselves when
they betrayed. They had to lie. Now the blood has gone thin in these last
generations of neoliberalism. These guys are dumb club members. So with Bonta,
it was just a straightforward and obvious lie, this time in the spotlight.

Now, I've been careful to say that it's an older generation of Democrats who
cosplay as substantive. One reason Lina Khan has a different valence is
because, to continue the analogy, she isn't an actor playing a doctor. She's a
surgeon, and it was shocking, confusing, exhilarating, and scary all at once
to see someone in policy actually playing with the big boys in a real way.

This cycle is going to see a bunch of new people elected. Last year is when
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani won, and he definitely is perceived to have a
different approach. How different is an important question. Abdul El-Sayed,
who is probably the most important figure, is quite smart. We [interviewed
him](https://www.organizedmoney.fm/p/a-conversation-with-abdul-el-sayed) for
Organized Money. Melat Kiros and Angie Nixon both prevailed on campaigns that
promised to break up big medicine and take on corporate concentration. So did
Aisha Wahab in California. In Arkansas, Hallie Shoffner is campaigning against
corporate concentration of farming. There will be more of this.

They may show a different form of politics, taking the side of the anti-
Ellison coalition, as it were. The point, though, is that what we just saw is
not just a battle we lost. It is a _prelude_ of the kind of tactics and
coalitions to come. Right now, it's clear that billionaires don't have to
follow the law. It's also clear there is now a serious challenge to that
framework. It wasn't quite powerful enough to block the merger. But now we
know how they are going to play the game, and they aren't going to be nice
about it.

And now, the rest of the round-up. There are a bunch of important stories. For
instance, cities are taking on surveillance pricing, teenage hackers are
extorting the FBI, and bond yields are way up, which means Wall Street is
saying there's not enough global cash for all the data centers and wars. Oh,
and it came out that Meta's legal team actually made hats bragging about how
they lie to the courts. All that after the paywall.
